title: When important work disappears between people and systems
linkedin:
Important work rarely disappears all at once.

It disappears one handover at a time.

An intake waits in an inbox. A reporting input sits with the wrong owner. A required document is found missing only when someone needs it. A manager asks for an update, and the team rebuilds the story from messages, spreadsheets and memory.

Capable people can work hard inside a workflow that still makes the next action difficult to see.

That is the problem Heutrix exists to help solve.

Heutrix grew from first-hand experience running a disability and allied health services organisation.

We help Australian disability support providers improve recurring non-clinical workflows. We also work with allied health practices facing the same operating pattern.

Our approach is simple:

- understand how the work happens now;
- clarify ownership, status, handovers and exceptions;
- choose the smallest useful improvement; and
- use technology only where it supports a defined result.

The answer may be Heutrix Diagnostics, Heutrix Workflow Transformation, Heutrix AI Guardrails—or an honest recommendation not to proceed.

Workflow first. Technology second.

Follow Heutrix for practical field notes on intake, reporting preparation, evidence and documents, handovers and responsible workplace AI.

Where does status become guesswork in your organisation? Keep the answer high level—no participant, worker, client or other sensitive information.

title: Before buying another tool, answer five workflow questions
linkedin:
“We need a new system” is often the first proposed solution.

It should be the sixth question.

Before choosing software, automation or AI, answer these five:

1. Trigger: what starts the work?
2. Owner: who is accountable for the next action?
3. Information: what is needed, and where should it live?
4. Exception: what happens when the normal path breaks?
5. Finish: what does done mean, and who confirms it?

If those answers are unclear, new technology can make the confusion move faster.

The smallest useful improvement may be:

- one agreed handover;
- a controlled status and next-action view;
- a simpler form;
- one stable automation;
- a lightweight internal tool; or
- no build at all.

That is the Heutrix principle: improve the workflow before adding technology.

If several workflows are competing for attention, use the free Workflow Bottleneck Scorecard to assess one at a time. The interactive tool suggests a next step from the friction, evidence and readiness you report. The accompanying PDF guide and workbook help you compare workflows. No email address is required.

Get the Scorecard: https://heutrix-website.heutrix.workers.dev/resources/workflow-bottleneck-scorecard

A self-assessment is a starting point, not a verified business case.

title: Seven signs a workflow depends on memory
linkedin:
Your workflow may be a shared memory disguised as a system.

Seven signs:

1. A manager has to ask several people for one update.
2. Staff keep side spreadsheets to make the main process usable.
3. The same information is copied into more than one place.
4. A waiting item is discovered only when someone chases it.
5. Work slows down when one key person is away.
6. “Done” means something different across the team.
7. Reporting begins with a manual clean-up before anyone trusts it.

None of these proves you need a new platform.

They do suggest one repeated workflow deserves a closer look.

Start small: choose one item that entered the process this week. Can the right person see its owner, status, next action, review date and finish without asking for the backstory?

If not, that is a useful place to begin.

Which sign would you inspect first? Keep examples general and leave participant, worker and confidential information out of the comments.

title: Participant intake rarely breaks in one dramatic moment
linkedin:
Participant intake rarely breaks in one dramatic moment.

It becomes harder to manage through a series of small, invisible handovers.

An enquiry arrives. Information is requested. A fit decision waits. Someone follows up. A start date is discussed. Another team needs to act.

At each step, the same five questions matter:

- What is the current status?
- Who owns the next action?
- What is the team waiting for?
- When should it be reviewed again?
- What outcome will close the item?

If the answers sit across inboxes, spreadsheets, chat messages and staff memory, the team may be busy while the workflow remains difficult to see.

This is not about putting every participant detail in a dashboard. A useful operating view can hold a controlled reference, owner, status, next action and review date while sensitive records remain in the approved source system.

Take one recent intake and mark each handover from enquiry to outcome.

Where did someone have to reconstruct the story? That is often the first design problem worth examining.

Use the free Enquiry-to-Service-Start Visibility Starter Kit to examine one handover. No email is required. Keep completed working documents in your approved systems.

title: “Starting soon” is not a service-commencement status
linkedin:
Illustrative operating view — not compliance or service-readiness assurance.

“Starting soon” is not a service-commencement status.

Neither is “almost ready”.

Those phrases hide the decisions an accountable person still needs to make.

A practical commencement view should show, at an appropriate level:

- the intended start date;
- the current owner;
- what is complete;
- what is still waiting;
- the next action and review date;
- any exception requiring a decision; and
- who confirms readiness under the provider’s approved process.

The workflow should not infer readiness from a green cell or a completed checklist. A named person still makes the accountable decision.

Nor does every sensitive record need to be copied into the view. Often the operating layer needs only enough controlled information to show what happens next.

Before the next commencement, finish this sentence:

Ready means ______, and ______ confirms it.

If the team completes the sentence differently, the issue is bigger than a missing reminder.

title: Illustrative: the best automation decision was not to build
linkedin:
Illustrative Heutrix application—not a client result.

The request sounds straightforward:

“Can we automate reminders for missing information?”

In this illustrative scenario, Heutrix Diagnostics identifies three problems:

- different teams disagree about what “complete” means;
- nobody owns the exception decision; and
- the data needed to trigger the reminder is not recorded consistently.

Automating now would send conflicting reminders faster.

The more useful first move is no build:

1. Agree one decision rule.
2. Name the person who approves exceptions.
3. Run a short baseline using non-sensitive operational data.
4. Reassess whether automation is still justified.

That is what good diagnosis should do: compare process clarification, a manual control, a lightweight workflow and automation—then recommend the smallest option supported by the evidence.

The value is the decision, even when the answer is “not yet”.

Save this question for the next automation request:

Is the rule stable enough to automate?

title: A workflow is not transformed when the build goes live
linkedin:
A workflow is not transformed when the build goes live.

The team still needs to test it, understand it and take ownership.

Heutrix Workflow Transformation follows four stages:

Diagnose — understand the current workflow, its boundary and the baseline or baseline plan. This is part of implementation; it does not require a separate Diagnostics purchase.

Triage — agree the future state, responsibilities, dependencies, controls and written acceptance criteria.

Build — implement the smallest useful improvement and test it with the people who will use it. That can mean changing the process or configuring existing systems; new software is only one option.

Handover — guide and train the team, transfer agreed access and documentation, and make ownership, maintenance and limitations clear.

Mapping and design happen before implementation. Testing happens before acceptance. Handover makes the improvement usable beyond the project.

The result is one bounded non-clinical workflow implemented, tested and handed over, within a written scope.

Save the four stages for the next time “go live” is treated as the finish line.

title: Five questions before staff use AI at work
linkedin:
“We have an approved AI account” does not tell a staff member whether this task is safe to do.

Before AI supports a work task, answer five questions:

1. Use: what exact task is approved?
2. Information: what may—and may not—enter the tool?
3. Tool: which product, plan, settings and account are approved for that use?
4. Review: who checks the output, and what must they test?
5. Record: where does the approved final version belong?

The same tool may be suitable for drafting a generic checklist from non-sensitive instructions and unsuitable for participant, worker or other personal information.

Start narrow. Test with non-sensitive or synthetic information. Keep a person accountable for the final output and the decision it supports.

AI should assist a defined workflow—not quietly become an unreviewed step inside it.

title: Can staff classify a proposed AI task?
linkedin:
Illustrative decision framework.

Your AI policy is tested when a staff member asks:

“Can I use it for this?”

A practical answer needs three clear pathways.

Approved

The task, tool, information boundaries, output use and human-review step have been assessed and recorded.

Prohibited

The use sits outside the organisation’s boundary—for example, entering personal or sensitive information into an unapproved public AI tool, or allowing AI to make an important decision without accountable human judgement.

Conditional / review required

The idea may have value, but a question about purpose, information, settings, access, retention, consequence or reviewer still needs an answer.

An unassessed use stays in review. A conditional decision must state what has to be resolved before use can proceed.

That third pathway matters. It gives staff somewhere safe to take a useful idea without assuming every new use is allowed—or forcing experimentation underground.

A short, maintained use-case register is more useful than a long policy nobody can apply.

Take one proposed administrative task and ask: which pathway is it in, who decided and when is it reviewed again? Use non-sensitive or synthetic information during assessment.

This is general operational guidance, not legal or privacy advice.

title: Removing the name does not automatically make an AI prompt safe
linkedin:
Removing the name does not automatically remove identification risk.

In a small team or unusual situation, the remaining context may still identify a person.

The OAIC recommends avoiding personal information, particularly sensitive information, in publicly available generative AI tools as a matter of best practice.

Before an administrative AI use proceeds, check its purpose, information, approved tool and settings, access, retention and accountable reviewer.

Use non-sensitive or synthetic information while assessing an idea, and obtain qualified advice where needed.

Read the OAIC guidance: https://www.oaic.gov.au/privacy/privacy-guidance-for-organisations-and-government-agencies/guidance-on-privacy-and-the-use-of-commercially-available-ai-products
